lesson.title: The P → F / FF Shift
lesson.subtitle: How English preserved what German transformed

hook.title: The Medieval Sound Wave
hook.content: Between 500 and 700 AD, a phonetic wave swept northward across the southern German highlands. English, safely isolated across the North Sea, preserved the ancient Germanic sounds. One of the cleanest rules: wherever English kept 'P', High German shifted it into 'F' or double 'FF'.

footnotes.title: The Second Sound Shift
footnotes.content: Also known as the High German Consonant Shift (Zweite Lautverschiebung), separating Low German/English from High German.

pattern.title: Post-Vocalic P becomes F / FF
pattern.content: After a vowel, English 'P' systematically becomes German 'F' or 'FF'. Hope becomes hoffen. Help becomes helfen. Sleep becomes schlafen. Ship becomes Schiff (a ship's captain is still called a skipper in English!). Ape becomes Affe. Ripe becomes reif (reifen means 'to ripen'). At the start of words, drop the German 'F' in 'PF-' to reveal the English twin: Pfad ↔ path, Pfund ↔ pound, Pfeffer ↔ pepper, Apfel ↔ apple!

footnotes.title: Gemination
footnotes.content: Short vowels triggered a double 'ff' (hoffen, Schiff), while long vowels and liquids took single 'f' (schlafen, helfen).

pattern.linguist_note: At the start of words, Germanic P shifted to PF (path → Pfad, pound → Pfund, pipe → Pfeife). After vowels, it shifted to F or FF (ship → Schiff, sleep → schlafen). English borrowed the Low German nautical word 'skipper' (literally 'Schiff-er', ship-master).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German verb for English 'hope' using the P → FF shift:
exercises.affirmation: You breathed the p into ff and pulled the ending on — the shift is becoming a reflex.
exercises.explanation: Post-vocalic P shifted into double FF + infinitive -en = hoffen.

exercises.prompt: Match the English words with their P → F/FF German cognates:
exercises.target_answer: Schiff, helfen, schlafen, Affe, Apfel, einsteigen, aussteigen
exercises.meaning: ship, to help, to sleep, ape, apple, to board, to get off
exercises.affirmation: Four p-words read straight through the shift — and the last two ride the modal bracket you built last topic.
exercises.explanation: English post-vocalic P regularly corresponds to German F or FF — and PF- opens the word in Apfel. einsteigen and aussteigen are the bracket infinitives from the last topic, back for another ride.

exercises.prompt: At the market stall: 'Der Apfel ist reif — aber zu teuer.' What consonant shift connects English 'ripe' and German 'reif'?
exercises.affirmation: You read reif backwards to ripe — every German f whispers its English p origin.
exercises.explanation: Voiceless stop P shifted into fricative F after a long vowel: ripe ↔ reif, on a fruit that is reif but, alas, zu teuer.

exercises.prompt: Apply the P → FF shift: English: 'sleep' → German verb:
exercises.affirmation: You heard schl- where English says sl-, and the p breathed into f — sleep became schlafen.
exercises.explanation: English sl- becomes schl- and p shifts to f.

exercises.idea: you hope your friend feels like coming along: I hope you have the craving (the Lust)
cues: Who hopes? → ich hoffe — hope is a regular verb here: hoff- + -e
Who has the Lust? → du hast Lust — hast is haben's du-form (have ↔ haben: the same ancient verb)
Run it straight through: no 'that', no comma between the two clauses
exercises.meaning: I hope you feel like it (have the craving)

vocab_hints.note: haben = to have — ich habe, du hast. English 'have' and German 'haben' are the same ancient verb; Lust = desire, the noun English kept as 'lust'

exercises.explanation: German lets 'I hope' run straight into 'you have the Lust' — no 'that', no comma. And hoffen is your P → F hope wearing a working ending.

summary.outcome: Use a familiar English p-word to help recognize related German f/ff words.

use_example.english: I hope you feel like it.

summary.takeaway: Every time you see German 'f' or 'ff' in a core word, test whether replacing it with 'p' creates an English word.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the PF- openers — path becomes Pfad, pound becomes Pfund: the word-initial explosion of the shift.

twist.prompt: Same hope, new cargo: this time you hope your friend is in — I hope you want to watch TV. Put it in German.
twist.explanation: Two clauses, so the full sentence takes a comma: Ich hoffe, du willst fernsehen. The modal willst takes the bare infinitive fernsehen at the end — no zu, no 'that' — and the person lives in willst, not in fernsehen.

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

schlafen.etymology_derivation: p → f with sl- → schl- cluster.

schiff.etymology_derivation: P → FF shift. Cognate with English "ship" and living nautical twin "skipper" (literally Schiff-er, ship-master).

pfeffer.context_phrase: Gib mir bitte Salz und Pfeffer.
pfeffer.context_translation: Please give me salt and pepper.
pfeffer.etymology_derivation: Double shift: initial p → pf and medial pp → ff.

pfad.etymology_derivation: Double shift: initial p → pf and th → d.

lust.context_translation: I feel like having ice cream.
lust.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lustuz — the explicit twin of English lust; in German it just means desire (Lust haben). [wiktionary]

teuer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *diurijaz — the true twin of English dear (d → t). [wiktionary]

fernsehen.etymology_derivation: fern + sehen — literally far-seeing; the entry calls it a calque of French télévision, the same idea as English television. [wiktionary]

einsteigen.context_phrase: Wir steigen in den Bus ein.
einsteigen.etymology_derivation: ein (in) + steigen (to climb): to climb in — German pictures boarding as climbing aboard; the climb-verb is native German. [wiktionary]

aussteigen.context_phrase: Ich steige an der nächsten Station aus.
aussteigen.context_translation: I get off at the next stop.
aussteigen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + steigen (to climb): to climb out and off the train, bus or tram. [wiktionary]

pforte.context_translation: We stand before the gate / portal.

schlafzimmer.context_translation: The child sleeps in the bedroom.
schlafzimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of Schlaf and Zimmer; schlafen corresponds to English sleep, with the medial p appearing as f in German. [wiktionary]

hüfte.context_phrase: Sie legt die Hände auf die Hüften.
hüfte.context_translation: She puts her hands on her hips.
hüfte.etymology_derivation: From Old High German huf, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz. English hip is a listed cognate, keeping the old p where High German shifted to f. [wiktionary]

würfel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wurpilaz, die, akin to *werpana, to throw — the same throw-family as English warp; the Germanic p surfaces as pf in German. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
